## Executive assessment

Avaddon is a useful case study because its history contains several different kinds of change. Email campaigns made the ransomware visible at scale. Threat reporting described encryption, threatened disclosure and threatened denial of service. Researchers identified a recovery opportunity that depended on the state of an infected system. Later, public decryption tools changed the options available to victims. None of those developments alone establishes that every organization recovered, every stolen copy disappeared or every participant stopped committing crime.

This study focuses on the documented 2020-2021 activity and recovery milestones. It deliberately avoids a single definitive launch date because the sources do not agree about the earliest observation. It also avoids combining message volume, published victim listings and released keys into a fictitious total. These quantities describe different things and arise from different collection methods.

The historical sections use original vendor observations, a technical research paper, official advisories and recovery-tool documentation. The longer operational sections are original defensive analysis and a fictional exercise, not an invented reconstruction of a named victim. They explain what decisions the evidence should support, what uncertainties remain, and what a response team should record before calling an incident closed.

No malware, stolen data or criminal service was accessed. No decryptor was downloaded or executed. This article offers no guarantee that a particular file collection can be recovered. It does not identify a convicted operator or attribute the shutdown to a specific government action. Its purpose is to make the research useful without converting uncertainty into a dramatic but unsupported story.

## Early visibility: a campaign count is not a victim count

Proofpoint's June 25, 2020 research described a renewed appearance of ransomware as an initial email payload. Within its observations, more than one million messages featured Avaddon between June 4 and June 10, including more than 750,000 on June 6. The June 4 campaign focused heavily on transportation organizations and school districts. Other reported targeting included manufacturing, education, media and entertainment. Photo-themed lures featured in the examples. [1]

These are message observations, not a count of encrypted computers or successfully compromised organizations. A campaign can send many messages to the same organization; a message can be blocked, ignored, investigated or executed. The reported scale establishes delivery pressure within the vendor's visibility, not a million completed ransomware incidents.

The distinction matters when turning research into presentation graphics. A large numeral labeled simply victims would change the meaning of the source. In this study, delivery volume stays attached to the June campaign window and the reporting vendor. No conversion rate is invented.

## Official warnings and incompatible origin dates

The Australian Cyber Security Centre's advisory, published May 8, 2021, describes Avaddon as ransomware-as-a-service and records impacts on Australian organizations. It identifies malicious email delivery, data-publication threats and DDoS threats, along with backup and patching recommendations. Its background says first detection occurred in February 2019. The live page also displays a later review date, June 17, 2026. [2]

NHS Digital's April 29, 2021 alert instead says first observation was in February 2020. It describes phishing and some exposed Remote Desktop Services delivery, with theft, encryption and DDoS threats. Its response advice includes isolation, backup testing and account protection. [3]

Neither date should silently replace the other. A reader cannot infer from these pages alone whether the difference reflects distinct definitions, an earlier sample, a reporting error or later editing. The June 2020 campaign is therefore used here as a clearly documented operational milestone rather than proof that no earlier activity existed. The study preserves publication dates and avoids pretending that current live pages are immutable snapshots of their original wording.

This is an evidence-management issue, not an excuse to ignore the threat. Defenders could act on the documented behavior without settling the exact birthday of the malware family. Historical writing should retain the disagreement until stronger evidence resolves it.

## Research recovery was conditional, not a break of modern encryption

Javier Yuste and Sergio Pastrana's February 2021 paper studies Avaddon and demonstrates a memory-based recovery approach. The relevant conditions are essential: key material had to remain available in memory or a suitable captured memory image, and the evaluation described an original version of an encrypted file for key identification. The authors tested particular samples, including one observed in January 2021, in a controlled virtual environment. [4]

Their findings concern key handling and implementation, not a general defeat of AES or RSA. The paper also discusses similarities to MedusaLocker as suggestive evidence rather than a definitive identity finding. Its discussion of exposed victim data expressly avoids downloading or validating that material.

The recovery approach created a time-sensitive forensic issue. A change to machine state could remove useful evidence. That is not a universal instruction to leave destructive software running: containment and preservation need qualified coordination. A dated experiment cannot be assumed to work against every subsequent build, every damaged file or every real-world environment.

## The reported June shutdown and what it did not establish

On June 16, 2021, the Czech national cybersecurity authority NÚKIB reported that Avaddon's operation had ended on June 11. Its notice attributed the initial key-release reporting to BleepingComputer, described the operator website as unavailable and said the reason for the shutdown was unknown. It pointed victims to Emsisoft's recovery tool. [5]

The authority's notice also contrasted published institution listings with a larger key-derived estimate. Those are not interchangeable measurements. This study does not reproduce them as an independently verified victim census, infer a payment rate or multiply them by a typical demand to estimate revenue.

The announcement supports describing a reported shutdown and recovery opportunity. It does not prove an arrest, prosecution, permanent exit from crime or erasure of stolen data. Even when an official publication relays a credible report, the chain of attribution remains relevant. Here the public notice is evidence of the authority's assessment and advice, not a claim that this research independently obtained or validated the released keys.

## Public recovery tools changed the practical options

Emsisoft's official Avaddon page dates version 2.1.0.0 to June 11, 2021. It describes the tool as free but supplied without warranty and cautions that tools may apply only to particular ransomware versions. The page says determination of the correct key can take up to a minute for the first encrypted file. This is documentation, not a performance result measured for this case study. [6]

The associated three-page guide emphasizes quarantining the malware first. It notes that connected and network drives can appear among default locations, and it retains encrypted files by default because exact equality with the original data cannot be guaranteed. Its log-saving feature provides a way to preserve the tool's reported outcome. No logs or files were uploaded to a third party for this study. [7]

Bitdefender's June 21, 2021 announcement describes an updated free decryptor following an earlier partial tool released in February. That chronology independently shows why recovery advice needs a date and a version. A later tool should not be confused with the earlier memory-dependent research method. Its availability does not establish successful recovery of all affected data. [8]

## Timeline with explicit evidence boundaries

| Milestone | Evidence | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| June 4-10, 2020 | Proofpoint reports high-volume Avaddon email delivery | Messages are not successful infections |
| February 2021 | Researchers publish conditional memory-based recovery | Sample and machine-state requirements apply |
| April 29, 2021 | NHS Digital publishes its alert | Origin date differs from the Australian record |
| May 8, 2021 | ACSC publishes campaign advisory | Live page was reviewed later; historical claims remain dated |
| June 11, 2021 | Emsisoft tool version is dated; shutdown later reported | Tool availability is not universal recovery |
| June 16, 2021 | NÚKIB describes reported shutdown and unknown cause | Not evidence of convictions or permanent eradication |
| June 21, 2021 | Bitdefender announces updated recovery tool | Distinct from its earlier partial offering |

The timeline is a sequence of reporting and recovery milestones. It is not a minute-by-minute intrusion chain. No single victim is asserted to have experienced every behavior listed in these sources.

## Analytical model: separate the pressures before choosing a response

The following sections are original defensive analysis. An organization facing several extortion pressures should begin by separating the harms rather than treating them as one technical problem. Encryption threatens the availability of data and services. Unauthorized copying threatens confidentiality. Network flooding threatens reachability. These harms can occur together, but a successful response to one does not automatically solve the others.

A practical incident board should assign an owner and an evidence question to each workstream. The availability owner asks which critical functions cannot operate, what dependencies they need and what recovery paths exist. The confidentiality owner asks what access and transfer evidence supports an exposure assessment. The network owner asks whether observed loss of service comes from hostile traffic, deliberate isolation, overloaded recovery systems or an unrelated fault.

This separation prevents urgency from distorting diagnosis. A threatening message that promises a DDoS attack is evidence of a threat. It is not by itself evidence that a flood is underway. Conversely, a service outage should not be dismissed merely because the attacker's claim is unverified. The team should inspect the service and its network path, establish observed symptoms and preserve the distinction between a claim and a measurement.

The same principle improves communication. Leadership can hear that essential files are being restored while exposure analysis continues and public-service stability remains under observation. Such a statement is more useful than either declaring everything solved or describing every system as equally lost. It identifies progress without giving assurance beyond the evidence.

A shared situation report should list dependencies between workstreams. Reconnecting a recovered application may expose it to unresolved access. Moving a large recovery dataset may strain a network already under pressure. Publishing incident details may reveal defensive work or sensitive affected-party information. Coordination is therefore necessary even when the technical problems are deliberately separated.

## Email volume should lead to exposure analysis, not inflated statistics

When a campaign reaches an organization, the response team needs a sequence of states rather than a single received-or-not label. Useful states include rejected at the gateway, delivered to a mailbox, accessed by a user, attachment retrieved, execution observed and further activity confirmed. The evidence available for each state differs. A mail trace may establish delivery while saying little about endpoint execution.

The organization should define its denominator before reporting percentages. A delivery rate might use unique messages; a user-impact rate might use unique accounts; an endpoint investigation might count distinct devices. Mixing those denominators can make a security control appear stronger or weaker than it is. Repeat sends and forwarded messages also need a consistent treatment if the team wants a meaningful comparison over time.

A campaign search can help locate related messages, but the result should not automatically label every recipient compromised. The team can prioritize investigation based on execution evidence, account privileges, device reach and business function. This approach allocates attention according to consequence while avoiding a blanket allegation against people who merely received an unwanted message.

Training should be equally specific. A photo-themed lure exploits curiosity or concern, but telling staff to be more careful is not a complete control. Organizations can provide a simple reporting route, make suspicious-message handling less burdensome and test attachment policies with harmless representative content. The goal is to reduce the number of risky decisions required of an individual, not to make a user the final barrier against every campaign.

A useful post-incident measure is the time between the first trustworthy report and the containment of related exposure. Another is whether the team can reconstruct the delivery-to-execution boundary. Neither requires pretending that every blocked message would otherwise have produced ransomware. Honest metrics make future investment decisions easier because they show which uncertainty or delay actually remains.

## Remote access deserves a separate investigation branch

An email-centered history can create tunnel vision. If a source describes multiple access paths, responders should keep plausible branches open until local evidence narrows them. The presence of phishing messages in a mailbox does not prove that those messages caused an intrusion. A separate remote-access event may have established the access that mattered.

A remote-access investigation should focus on identity, authentication context and the authority granted by the session. The team needs to know which account was used, whether its use was expected, what systems became reachable and whether access persisted after the initial session ended. The evidence may include authorized logs and configuration records; missing records should be listed as a limitation rather than filled with an assumed story.

Remediation should address the observed authority, not just the visible connection. Changing one password may be inadequate if another account or active session remains available. Removing an unfamiliar account may be premature if the team has not established its owner and purpose. A controlled investigation can preserve useful evidence while distinguishing legitimate administration from unauthorized changes.

Business continuity also matters. If an organization relies on remote administration to restore services, shutting down every channel without a replacement may impede recovery. The response plan should define a trusted administrative route with limited scope and accountable operators. That route should be evaluated independently of the compromised path instead of assuming that the old workflow remains trustworthy once a warning disappears.

The historical family name is secondary to these questions. A system should not be declared clean because the currently observed access pattern differs from a popular summary of Avaddon. Local evidence determines the incident's scope; historical research provides hypotheses and context.

## The preservation dilemma is a decision, not a slogan

Time-sensitive recovery research can conflict with a reflexive shutdown response. Preserving volatile evidence may retain a recovery option, while allowing an infected environment to continue operating may cause further harm. There is no responsible universal answer that ignores the specific system, the available expertise and the containment capability.

A mature plan assigns this decision before an incident occurs. It names who can assess active harm, who can preserve evidence safely and who accepts the business consequence of a particular action. It distinguishes network isolation from power-state changes and defines how to escalate when the team cannot confidently contain activity. The plan should never require an untrained user to improvise live malware handling.

The incident record should capture the decision time, observed state, available options and rationale. If evidence could not be preserved because immediate harm required a different action, that should be documented honestly. If preservation was attempted, the record should identify what was captured and what completeness checks were possible. A vague statement that forensics was done does not establish that the needed material exists.

Preserved material is itself sensitive. Memory and disk evidence can contain credentials, personal information and confidential business data. Handling should be limited to authorized people and approved storage, with a clear retention purpose. A useful recovery possibility is not permission to upload an entire image to an arbitrary online service or share it in a public support forum.

Tabletop exercises can expose gaps without creating a real infection. A facilitator can provide a synthetic notice that a recovery option depends on evidence that may soon be lost. Participants must decide how to contain harm, seek qualified help and record uncertainty. The exercise should assess the decision process, not reward a technically dramatic maneuver that would be unsafe in production.

## Distinguish recovery mechanisms before making a promise

A public decryptor can exist for different reasons. A researcher may identify an implementation weakness; a later event may make key material available; a vendor may support only certain formats or builds. A recovery summary should therefore record not just that a tool exists but what problem it addresses and what prerequisites its official documentation states.

This distinction is operationally important because old advice can remain searchable long after it stops being complete. A responder may find a dated statement that recovery requires a particular machine state and assume that no other route exists. Another may find a newer tool and incorrectly assume that its existence invalidates every earlier limitation. The correct approach is to preserve the chronology while evaluating the tool relevant to the affected material.

Before a recovery attempt, an authorized owner should define the input collection and the acceptance criteria. The collection needs provenance: where the files came from, whether they have been modified, whether more than one affected system contributed them and whether a known-good copy exists. These facts help distinguish a tool mismatch from preexisting corruption or an incomplete collection.

Acceptance criteria should reflect business meaning. A file that opens may still contain damaged records or incomplete transactions. A database may need application-level consistency checks. A document archive may need representative content review. Exact comparison with a trusted original is valuable when available, but its absence should be recorded rather than concealed behind a successful status message.

Recovery should begin with controlled copies and a representative subset. The organization can then evaluate failure patterns, time requirements and storage needs before expanding the attempt. This is a recommendation for an authorized recovery workflow, not a claim that this study ran a tool or verified a vendor's success rate.

## Backups and decryptors are complementary options

The existence of a free recovery tool should not erase the value of a clean backup. Backups may provide a more predictable path for some datasets, while a decryptor may help with material not covered by an acceptable restore point. A recovery plan can compare both options without treating either as a universal guarantee.

The comparison should include the age of the data, the trustworthiness of the copy, the dependencies of the application and the cost of validating the result. A recent backup that is inaccessible through damaged infrastructure may not be immediately useful. A decrypted dataset may require extensive checks before it can support operations. The quickest technical action is not always the quickest route to a reliable business service.

Restoration priorities should be agreed with service owners. A large archive may be less urgent than a small configuration dataset that enables several essential systems. Conversely, a seemingly minor record set may be needed to reconcile transactions and avoid downstream errors. Mapping these dependencies before an incident reduces the pressure to choose based only on file size or executive visibility.

A recovery environment should remain separated from unresolved compromise. Rebuilding an application while reusing untrusted credentials or administrative paths can reintroduce risk. The recovery team should document the basis for trusting its infrastructure, accounts and software sources. A decryptor operates on data; it does not certify the surrounding system as safe.

Finally, preserve the ability to revise the plan. A partial result may justify a hybrid approach, using backups for some information and carefully validated recovered files for other material. The decision log should identify which source produced each dataset so later discrepancies can be investigated. Without that provenance, a rapid restoration can become a prolonged integrity problem.

## Shutdown reporting should not close victim investigations

The disappearance of an operator service can be encouraging without resolving a victim's exposure. A particular organization still needs to determine what happened locally, whether access remains and what information may have left its control. An ecosystem event is not a substitute for those findings.

The word shutdown also invites causal speculation. It can be tempting to connect a disappearance to a nearby policy announcement, a law-enforcement operation or a major incident involving another group. Unless the evidence establishes that connection, a case study should not turn chronology into causation. The stronger statement is often that a service became unavailable and the reason remained unknown in the cited account.

Likewise, a new name in later reporting does not automatically prove a rebrand. Code similarities, shared infrastructure, common recruitment patterns and participant overlap can support different hypotheses. A responsible analysis states which kind of link is observed and what alternative explanations remain. This study does not claim an unbroken organizational identity beyond the available record.

For victims, closure should be based on explicit criteria. Those can include restoration of essential services, investigation of observed access, assessment of exposure, preservation of necessary evidence and assignment of unresolved risks. Different workstreams may close at different times. The overall report should make that visible instead of forcing one dramatic end date onto a complex recovery.

The same care applies to public statements. It may be accurate to say that recovery has progressed following the availability of a tool. It is a different and much stronger claim to say that all consequences have ended. Communications should distinguish the result the organization has tested from the reassurance it hopes will eventually be justified.

## A practical evidence register for conflicting claims

An evidence register makes these distinctions repeatable. Each important claim should have a source, publication date, observed period, scope and confidence statement. A separate field should record whether the source reports its own observations or relays another party's account. This prevents an official citation from accidentally making a secondhand claim look independently verified.

For numerical claims, the register should state the unit. Messages, files, keys, devices, organizations and payments belong in different columns, not one victims field. If a relationship between units is unknown, the analyst should record unknown rather than invent a conversion. The temptation to produce a neat chart is not a reason to manufacture comparability.

For technical claims, the register should identify the tested sample or version scope where the source supplies it. A behavior seen in one build can guide investigation while remaining narrower than a family-wide assertion. The absence of a behavior in a brief summary also does not prove the malware lacked that capability. Reading scope matters as much as citation count.

For changing recovery guidance, the register should preserve both the earlier statement and the later development. The later entry can supersede practical advice without rewriting what was known at the earlier date. This is especially useful for training material, where an old slide may otherwise continue circulating after the underlying recovery landscape has changed.

The register should also include a not-verified column. In this study that includes successful recovery of a victim collection, a complete victim census, the reason for the shutdown and a definitive operator identity. Explicit limitations give the next researcher a useful starting point. They are more informative than leaving readers to infer that every unmentioned question was settled.

## Fictional tabletop: three pressures and a recovery announcement

This exercise concerns a fictional regional service company. It uses synthetic messages, invented logs and harmless sample files. No malware is executed and no criminal site is contacted. The aim is to test coordination and evidence discipline, not to recreate a specific historical victim.

During the first twenty minutes, participants receive a service-outage report, an extortion message and a mail-system campaign summary. They must separate observed symptoms from attacker claims, establish owners for availability and confidentiality, and identify which evidence could connect delivery to execution. The facilitator should challenge any assertion that every message recipient is compromised.

During the next twenty minutes, a remote-access log introduces a second plausible entry path. The team must decide what can be concluded, what additional authorized evidence is needed and which access controls can be changed without destroying essential recovery capability. A successful team retains competing hypotheses rather than forcing all observations into the first explanation.

The next stage introduces a dated technical paper and a newer public recovery-tool announcement. Participants must compare the recovery mechanisms, identify prerequisites and select a safe evaluation plan. They should explain why preservation, containment and application validation require separate decisions. No points are awarded for assuming a tool works merely because its title matches the ransom note.

In the final stage, a news summary says the criminal operation has shut down. Leadership asks whether the incident can be declared over. Participants must produce a concise update that separates restored functions, unresolved exposure, remaining access questions and the meaning of the shutdown report. The exercise ends with assigned actions, evidence owners and review dates rather than a fictional guarantee of complete recovery.

## Conclusion

Avaddon's history demonstrates why ransomware research should follow evidence through time. Delivery observations, technical weaknesses, official warnings and later tools answer different questions. Combining them carelessly produces an impressive-looking story that can mislead both readers and responders.

The strongest practical lesson is disciplined separation: distinguish messages from infections, keys from organizations, threatened harm from observed harm, recovery tools from successful recovery, and a reported shutdown from eradication. These distinctions do not weaken a case study. They make its recommendations usable when a real organization must decide what to do next.

## Source register and reading scope

1. [Proofpoint, Ransomware Families as an Initial Payload Reemerges, June 25, 2020](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/security-briefs/ransomware-initial-payload-reemerges-avaddon-philadelphia-mr-robot-and-more). Overview and Avaddon campaign section read; counts remain vendor-observed messages.
2. [ACSC, 2021-003: Ongoing campaign using Avaddon Ransomware](https://www.cyber.gov.au/advisory/2021-003-ongoing-campaign-using-avaddon-ransomware). Background, techniques and mitigations read; live publication and review dates retained.
3. [NHS Digital, Avaddon Ransomware, April 29, 2021](https://digital.nhs.uk/cyber-alerts/2021/cc-3833). Summary, delivery, activity and remediation sections read; inconsistent origin date noted.
4. [Yuste and Pastrana, Avaddon ransomware: an in-depth analysis and decryption of infected systems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.04796). Relevant introduction, recovery, experiment and conclusion sections read in extracted text; not every reverse-engineering instruction reproduced or tested.
5. [NÚKIB, Ukončení činnosti ransomwaru Avaddon, June 16, 2021](https://nukib.gov.cz/cs/infoservis/aktuality/1722-ukonceni-cinnosti-ransomwaru-avaddon/). Substantive Czech notice read and summarized in English; relayed reporting and unknown cause retained.
6. [Emsisoft, Avaddon decryptor](https://www.emsisoft.com/en/ransomware-decryption/avaddon). Version date, general limitations and first-file note checked; tool not executed.
7. [Emsisoft, Avaddon usage guide](https://www.emsisoft.com/en/ransomware-decryption/howtos/emsisoft_howto_avaddon.pdf). Three-page guide read in extracted text; preservation and scope cautions retained.
8. [Bitdefender, New Bitdefender Decryptor for Avaddon Infections, June 21, 2021](https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/labs/new-bitdefender-decryptor-for-avaddon-infections). Announcement read; partial and updated tools distinguished.

Sources were reviewed as of 16 November 2026. An attempted retrieval of the original FBI advisory was unavailable and is not represented as a source read. No live malware test, recovery guarantee or criminal-site access was performed.
